chunks.content: 1. Introduction In 2009, the World Health Organization (WHO) added snakebites to the list of neglected diseases, and antisnake venom was included in the list of essential drugs. To date, the available epidemiological data on snakebites are still incomplete and inaccurate [ ]. Current and up-to-date articles on snakebites and their treatment in European children are lacking in literature, even though there are over 5 million cases of snakebites each year [ ]. The relatively low amount of data about snakebites in Europe likely contributes to a lack of sufficient interest in the issue, also indicated by the absence of mandatory reporting and the standardization of notification by health services [ ]. Furthermore, epidemiological data on snakebites are often unreliable, as most bites occur in rural areas where medical facilities are scarce, and many victims seek treatment from traditional healers. As a result, the number of cases indicated in hospital records is lower than the actual number [ ]. Snakebite envenoming is a rare but potentially fatal event, killing between 81,000 and 138,000 people each year and leaving another 400,000 people worldwide with permanent disabilities [ ]. Globally, most cases are caused by species from the Elapidae and Viperidae families [ ]. One-quarter of all viper bites in Europe occur without venom inoculation (dry bites) and clinical consequences, but lead to alarmism in the patient and physicians [ , ]. In the remaining three-quarters of cases, the injection of venom causes predominantly local symptoms. However, systemic symptoms may be present due to the venom’s lymphatic and blood diffusion. Furthermore, symptoms of viper-bite envenomation vary depending on the anatomical site involved, the amount and characteristics of the venom and the general condition of the victim [ ]. Snakebite envenoming in children, although proportionally less frequent, is generally more severe and often results in worse outcomes [ ]. Children are at higher risk compared to adults due to their smaller body size [ ]. In this narrative review, we describe the state of the art regarding snake envenomation in Europe and the related clinical framework and management of viper bites in children. Indeed, recognizing the clinical characteristics of a viper bite has a key role in prompt recognition and adequate treatment with anti-viper serum and supportive care. 2. Geographical and Epidemiologic Characteristics of Snakebite More than 95% of snakebite cases occur in tropical settings, particularly in South Asia, sub-Saharan Africa and South America, with the highest percentages occurring in low-income rural populations and children [ ]. In tropical countries, snakebites are considered an occupational hazard for agricultural workers, with the highest incidence and mortality reported in southern (121,000 cases and 14,000 deaths per year) and Southeast Asia (111,000 cases and 790 deaths per year) [ ]. In contrast, the USA records around 9000 cases and 5 deaths per year [ ]. The incidence of snakebites in Europe is lower than in the rest of the world (0.22–1.43 affected individuals per 100,000 people per year) [ ], and lethality is reduced due to the high quality of public health systems in these countries and the lower lethality of native snakes compared to their foreign counterparts [ ]. In Italy, the incidence can reach 5 per 100,000, with morbidity around 1 per 100,000 and a mortality rate of 0.1–0.2%. The Italian National Health Institute reports only one case of death due to venomous snakebites between 2003 and 2006 [ ], and a more recent Italian case series declared no mortality in children [ ]. Venomous snakes are classified into four families: Viperidae, Atractaspididae, Elapidae and Colubridae. Viperidae consist of more than 200 species, among which are some of the most dangerous snakes to human beings, including the Russell’s viper, the carpet viper, the puff adder, rattlesnakes and lance-head pit vipers [ ]. Viperidae are distributed over the Americas, Europe, Africa and Asia [ ]. The genus Vipera belongs to the “true vipers” and includes more than 20 species, occurring in virtually every country in Europe, except for some large islands such as the Balearics, Corsica, Crete, Malta and Sardinia [ ]. Venomous snakes in Europe all belong to the genus Vipera and are all true vipers [ ], unlike their American counterparts, which include pit vipers [ , ]. The species Vipera berus is the most common European viper, followed by Vipera ammdytes , Vipera aspis and Vipera ursinii , [ , ]. Vipera ( V. ) aspis is the most common viper in Italy, while V. ursinii is most common on the Apennines [ , ]. European vipers have peculiar characteristics useful for their identification, such as an average size of 50−70 cm, a vertical pupil which in bright light assumes a slit shape, at least one row of subocular scales, small scales irregularly arranged covering the top of the head, dorsal keeled

pit vipers [ , ]. The species Vipera berus is the most common European viper, followed by Vipera ammdytes , Vipera aspis and Vipera ursinii , [ , ]. Vipera ( V. ) aspis is the most common viper in Italy, while V. ursinii is most common on the Apennines [ , ]. European vipers have peculiar characteristics useful for their identification, such as an average size of 50−70 cm, a vertical pupil which in bright light assumes a slit shape, at least one row of subocular scales, small scales irregularly arranged covering the top of the head, dorsal keeled scales of the trunk and a triangular or sub-oval head shape [ ]. In a recent systematic review, a precise identification of the snake, indicating the genus and species, was reported for 56.8% of snakebites in Europe, and the most involved taxon was V. berus (63.3%), followed by V. ammodytes (17.7%), V. aspis (11.7%), V. latastei (4.0%), V. ursinii (2.6%) and V. seoanei (0.7%) [ ]. As snakebites are more prevalent in the summer and during the rainy season in association with agricultural activities, they can be classified as occupational diseases [ ]. In Europe, most of the snakebites occurred in June (75.7%) and accidentally, while working, walking or playing in a rural area. In 22.7% of cases, the bite occurred while the victim was catching or feeding a pet snake [ ]. Male gender, living in rural areas, summer months and daytime are the main risk factors for viper bites [ ]. Although snakebites can occur at any age, an Italian survey showed that they are more common in pre-pubertal children, with an average age of 6.5 years, due to their outdoor activities. Prevalence is lower in preschoolers (0–5 years), and children under 3 are generally spared as they stay at home and are usually accompanied by caregivers when outside [ ]. 3. Pathogenesis and Clinical Characteristics of Snakebite in Children in Europe Snakes inject their venom subcutaneously or intramuscularly, rarely intravenously [ ]. The pathogenesis of Vipera snakebites varies according to different venom compositions. In particular, the main Vipera toxins are as follows: Phospholipase A2, responsible for hemolysis, neurotoxicity, myotoxicity, cardiotoxicity, cytotoxicity, anticoagulation, convulsions, hypotension and inflammation; Snake venom serine proteinases (thrombin-like enzymes) and snake venom metalloproteinases, leading to local and systemic hemorrhages, although some classes of snake venom metalloproteinases may also cause procoagulant and pro-inflammatory activities; Snake C-type lectin-like proteins, with anticoagulant and platelet-modulating activities; Disintegrins, responsible for cell adhesion, migration, apoptosis, platelet aggregation and angiogenesis [ , , , , , ]. Generally, viperid venoms mainly induce hemotoxic and cytotoxic symptoms, more rarely neurotoxic effects [ ], which typically follow Elapidae bites [ ]. The hemorrhagic effect is caused by direct interference with the coagulation cascade and the consumption of platelets and coagulation factors at the site of injection [ ]. The neurotoxic effect is due to phospholipase A2 neurotoxins, which could be in the venom of V. ammodytes and some populations of V. aspis [ , ]. The severity of clinical manifestations depends on factors such as the snake size, the number of bites, the nature, location and depth of the bite and the amount of venom injected [ ]. The symptoms also depend on the involved viper species because of the different toxicological profiles [ ]. Therefore, the identification of the offending snake species may predict the clinical course. The identification of the species in Europe is facilitated by the fact that many areas of Europe are inhabited by only one species of venomous snake, especially in Northern and Central Europe [ ]. However, the composition of snake venom can vary within genera and even within species due to ontogeny and geographical distribution, making the clinical evolution of snakebites unpredictable [ ]. Although the variability in snake venom composition and lethality within the same species and/or for a given species is known, the lethal dose 50 of all viper snakes usually ranges from 1.0 to 2.0 mg/kg [ ]. The venom glands of adult specimens of V. ammodytes have 10–45 mg of venom, and one bite can excrete as much as 20 mg of venom, which can be a lethal dose, especially for children and patients with chronically illnesses [ ]. Indeed, due to their lower weight-to-venom ratio, children are more susceptible to the potentially fatal effects of snakebites; this can also lead to more fast and severe neurotoxicity, coagulopathy and severe local tissue damage [ ]. Furthermore, female gender, intense pain at onset, being bitten in the afternoon, elevated glycemia and an upper-extremity location are associated with high-grade envenomation in children [ ]. The first skin manifestation of viper envenomation is 1–2 distinct holes caused by the fangs [ ] ( ). In a systematic review of 3574 European studies (including 28 studies

and patients with chronically illnesses [ ]. Indeed, due to their lower weight-to-venom ratio, children are more susceptible to the potentially fatal effects of snakebites; this can also lead to more fast and severe neurotoxicity, coagulopathy and severe local tissue damage [ ]. Furthermore, female gender, intense pain at onset, being bitten in the afternoon, elevated glycemia and an upper-extremity location are associated with high-grade envenomation in children [ ]. The first skin manifestation of viper envenomation is 1–2 distinct holes caused by the fangs [ ] ( ). In a systematic review of 3574 European studies (including 28 studies of children and teenagers), evidence of fang marks was present in 90.5% of cases; 98.3% of snakebites involved the limbs, and the upper limbs were the most involved anatomic site (53.1%) [ ]. Venom cytotoxicity induces the disruption of blood vessel integrity, causing the appearance of local signs after 30 min, including edema (73.6% of cases), ecchymosis (68.4%) and erythema (56.6%) [ , ]. Loco-regional adenopathy was reported in 42.7% of cases [ ]. Skin and muscular necrosis, hives, purpura, petechiae and acute compartment syndrome may appear in later stages [ , , ]. Compartment syndrome occurs rarely but can cause ischemic damage to nerves and muscles, with irreversible tissue loss if not treated with a prompt fasciotomy [ ]. However, the onset of compartment syndrome may take several hours or even days to develop after snakebite, requiring careful monitoring over time. The lack of reliable predictors for compartment syndrome makes management challenging and costly. In a retrospective study, Hsu CP et al. [ ] identified elevated white blood cell counts and aspartate aminotransferase levels as risk factors for the development of compartment syndrome in 136 snakebitten adults. Although rare, lymphatic and blood toxicity can lead to systemic complications which can be life-threatening [ ]. Fever, headache, skin rash, vomiting and diarrhea are the most common systemic symptoms, but coagulopathy, bleeding, hypovolemia, acute kidney injury, cranial nerve neurotoxicity, dysesthesia/paresthesia and cardiac ischemia can also be observed [ , ]. In severe cases, hypovolemia secondary to coagulopathy, capillary leakage, and vasoactive and myocardial-depressing toxins may cause cardiovascular shock [ ]. Although neurological consequences following viper envenomation are uncommon in children, the involvement of the III, IV and VI cranial nerves may cause ptosis, diplopia and chewing disorder [ ]. Other neurological symptoms such as segmental dysesthesia or paresthesia occurred rarely [ ]. Neurological symptoms appear at least 11 h after the bite even in adults with mild local symptoms, while in children, neurotoxicity is always associated with extensive local effects [ ]. A rare case of spherocytosis with severe intravascular hemolysis, hemoglobinemia and hemoglobinuria after a V. ammodytes viper bite in an adult farmer was recently reported in Greece. The observed laboratory changes (rapid fall in hematocrit, along with hyperbilirubinemia, hemoglobinuria, absent haptoglobin and a marked increase in lactic dehydrogenase) were consistent with intravascular hemolysis, but the hematological picture was consistent with spherocytic rather than microangiopathic hemolysis [ ]. To date, no similar cases have been described in children. A grading system for assessing the severity of viper envenoming can be used as a guideline in research and in certain clinical settings. Based on the severity of viper bites, Audebert et al. [ ] developed a scale, which Boels et al. [ , ] later modified, identifying four grades: - Grade 0 (no envenoming): traces of bite and local signs. - Grade 1 (mild envenoming): local edema and absence of systemic symptoms. - Grade 2 (moderate envenoming): extensive regional edema, hypotension, vomiting, diarrhea. - Grade 3 (severe envenoming): persistent hypotension or shock, hemorrhage. In 2021, Marano et al. [ ] proposed a grading severity score adjusted for pediatric patients (pGSS) with relative management indications, which could be a useful tool for emergency pediatricians. In the aforementioned systematic review, grade 2 was the most frequently reported grade of envenomation (42.2%), followed by grade 1 (32.3%), grade 3 (13.9%) and grade 0 (11.7%) [ ]. 4. Long-Term Consequences of Snakebite in Children Most snakebite patients are not followed up with after they have been discharged from the hospital and the acute effects have resolved. Nevertheless, snakebites can also lead to long-term consequences, defined as conditions that persist or manifest more than six weeks after envenomation [ ]. Waiddanatha et al. [ ], in their systematic review of 51 studies conducted on adults and children in different countries around the world, described the long-term effects of snake envenomation. These effects include disabilities resulting from amputations, deformities, contractures and chronic ulceration, with malignant changes being rare. However, such complications are mostly related to bites from African and Asian cobras, and Central and South American pit vipers [ ]. Similarly, bites from Russell’s viper in Sri Lanka, India and Myanmar were associated with the progression of

as conditions that persist or manifest more than six weeks after envenomation [ ]. Waiddanatha et al. [ ], in their systematic review of 51 studies conducted on adults and children in different countries around the world, described the long-term effects of snake envenomation. These effects include disabilities resulting from amputations, deformities, contractures and chronic ulceration, with malignant changes being rare. However, such complications are mostly related to bites from African and Asian cobras, and Central and South American pit vipers [ ]. Similarly, bites from Russell’s viper in Sri Lanka, India and Myanmar were associated with the progression of acute kidney injury to chronic renal failure, as well as endocrine issues like delayed hypopituitarism [ , ]. Long-term psychological effects (depression, post-traumatic stress disorder and somatization), as well as long-term neurological complications like ptosis, were also described in children [ ], but these too are not associated with European viper bites. To date, no long-term sequelae have been reported in literature after European viper bites in children [ ], even after an acute phase characterized by compartment syndrome [ ]. 5. Diagnosis of Snakebite Envenomation The diagnosis of snakebite envenomation includes a thorough patient history, a targeted examination and appropriate laboratory testing. A detailed history includes information about the circumstances of the bite (geography, time of incident, activity and number of bites), details about the snake (if seen, carried or photographed), clinical manifestations of envenomation (including time of onset), first aid administered and past medical history (allergies, previous snakebites, pertinent medications and pre-existing medical conditions) [ ]. Hematologic changes are consistently observed after viper bites, likely as a response to the toxins or acute stress [ ]. Laboratory testing includes a blood coagulation profile and complete blood count to screen for venom-induced coagulopathies and anemia induced by internal bleeding. Other laboratory tests are useful in identifying complications, such as creatine kinase, electrolyte, urea and creatinine/nitrogen levels, which, together with urinalysis, can be used to evaluate venom-induced rhabdomyolysis and associated complications, such as myoglobinuric renal failure or polyuria, oliguria or anuria [ ]. In case of a viper bite, the recommended blood tests every 6 h for 24 h include those for hemocoagulation, blood count, urinalysis, hepatic tests, renal function, electrolytes, lactate dehydrogenase and creatine phosphokinase. Furthermore, laboratory tests help to assess the severity of envenoming and, thereby, the need for antivenom [ ]. In literature, leukocytosis associated with increased neutrophils is associated with the clinical severity of viper envenomation in children [ ]. It is also the major hematological change in a case report of a child with acute compartment syndrome needing fasciotomy after a bite by V. walser in the north of Italy [ ]. A study by Ozay et al. [ ] involving 77 children bitten by venomous snakes in Turkey found that 21% had thrombocytopenia (<120,000/mm 3 ), and 54% had leukocytosis. Additionally, the study revealed elevated levels of aspartate aminotransferase, lactate dehydrogenase and creatine phosphokinase and an increased prothrombin time, while the mean activated partial thromboplastin time was lower than the normal range. The platelet count was found to be inversely related to the severity of the grading score and the length of hospitalization [ ]. Digital oximetry and an electrocardiogram are also recommended [ ]. 6. Pediatric Management of Snakebite 6.1. Pre-Hospital Care In a pre-hospital setting, the rapid transport of the child to the nearest medical facility is the priority. It is important to keep the child calm and comfortable, as a hyperdynamic state can accelerate venom spread [ ]. Practices such as incision, suction devices, snake stones, cryotherapy and tourniquets should be avoided [ ] as they are not supported by scientific evidence and can delay medical attention, alter the clinical presentation and increase the risk of complications [ ]. Tourniquets are often still applied in rural settings, but they can increase local tissue destruction and cause gangrene [ ]. Pressure immobilization bandages are useful for elapid bites (which do not cause local swelling) to reduce lymph flow, but are not recommended for viperid bites because excessive pressure can sometimes worsen local tissue damage. Therefore, the WHO does not recommend pressure bandages for most snakebites, although limb immobilization plays a key role in treatment for all snakebites [ ]. The affected limb should be immobilized in a functional position, ideally below the level of the heart, to reduce the lymphatic absorption of the venom [ ]. Therefore, in a pre-hospital setting, the only beneficial actions include cleansing the wound with water and alcohol-free detergents, removing any constricting objects (e.g., jewelery, watches) that might impede blood circulation in case of swelling and applying a mild immobilization bandage, applied solely by emergency personnel [ ]. Immediate medical attention should be sought to ensure airway patency and provide adequate respiratory support, while preventing the aspiration

in treatment for all snakebites [ ]. The affected limb should be immobilized in a functional position, ideally below the level of the heart, to reduce the lymphatic absorption of the venom [ ]. Therefore, in a pre-hospital setting, the only beneficial actions include cleansing the wound with water and alcohol-free detergents, removing any constricting objects (e.g., jewelery, watches) that might impede blood circulation in case of swelling and applying a mild immobilization bandage, applied solely by emergency personnel [ ]. Immediate medical attention should be sought to ensure airway patency and provide adequate respiratory support, while preventing the aspiration of vomit or fluids [ ]. 6.2. Hospital Care Upon arrival at the hospital, an ABCDE approach should be followed. A detailed history should be taken, including the time of the incident and a description of the snake. First aid measures should be reviewed, and the patient’s general medical history, including any food or drug allergies, should be assessed [ ]. Minimal or no pain without additional symptoms suggests a dry bite; in this case, a 6 h observation period may be recommended [ ]. Significant neurologic impairment could require prompt intubation and ventilation [ ]. 6.3. Immunotherapy The WHO and the South East Asian Region Organization guidelines defined treatment for viper bites [ ]. Immunotherapy, which includes anti-viper serums, is the cornerstone of treatment for viper bites and is prescribed in case of at least grade 1 envenomation [ ]. Antivenoms are preparations of immunoglobulins or immunoglobulin fragments arranged by immunizing large animals (horses or sheep) with snake venom. After blood collection and plasma separation, antibodies are purified and preparations formulated to have a standard neutralizing potency against venoms used in immunization [ ]. Available antisera are generally manufactured by local facilities that create antivenoms specific for the viper species populating the area [ ]. Indications for administering antivenom (equine Fab or ovine Fab) include the following: circulatory instability unresponsive to treatment, rapid progression of swelling or bruising, prolonged or recurrent gastrointestinal symptoms, mucosal swelling, fluctuating consciousness and nerve paralysis (peripheral or cranial) [ ]. In borderline cases, the following conditions may further support the need for antivenom: leukocytosis (>15–20 × 10⁹/L), metabolic acidosis, hemolysis, coagulation issues and electrocardiographic abnormalities [ ]. The anti-viper serum might be administered within four hours after the bite but is still effective if taken within twenty-four hours [ ]. Identifying the snake species would be desirable in order to choose the most suitable antivenom. When the offending snake species is known, monovalent antivenoms may be administered, while polyvalent antivenoms are useful in cases of unidentified snake species. However, the relative proportion of antibodies to the target toxin in a polyvalent antivenom is often not as high as in a monovalent antivenom for a given snake species, resulting in reduced efficacy. Therefore, a higher dose of a polyvalent antidote may be required than of a monovalent one, resulting in increased costs and the risk of developing adverse reactions. Unfortunately, polyvalent antivenoms are often preferred, both because of the lack of monovalent antivenoms and because of the difficulty in identifying with certainty the offending snake [ ]. When a polyvalent antivenom is not available, monovalent antivenoms may be administered, exploiting their cross-reactivity [ ]. Indeed, antivenom raised against venom from one species can be effective against venoms from other vipers indigenous to Europe [ ], because most antivenom serums can neutralize the venoms of multiple snake species [ ]. The antivenom derived from the venom of V. ammodytes , V. berus and V. aspis seems to be the best option for treating viper bites in Italy as well as in Europe, where these species of vipers occur [ ]. The composition of snake venom and the protein sequences of homologous toxins are generally characterized by considerable diversity [ ]. Recent genetic and proteomic analyses showed that PLA2 components were found in both V. aspis and V. berus venom, but only those contained in V. aspis venom are neurotoxic [ ]. Therefore, PLA2 present in venoms of different species could be functionally and antigenically different and therefore variably susceptible to neutralization by available antisera. A recent Italian study investigated the toxicological profile of V. aspis and V. berus venoms and the effectiveness of two monovalent antivenoms in vivo in mice. The two antivenoms tested effectively counteract the effect of V. berus venom, but only partially neutralize the neurotoxicity of V. aspis , supporting the use of polyvalent antivenoms [ ]. Therefore, the use of polyvalent antivenoms against numerous species and subspecies of vipers could represent an interesting strategy for the more effective management of European snakes. Furthermore, small-molecule inhibitors that target the activity of the main toxic components of venoms can also be taken into account for the development of new broad-spectrum antivenoms [ ]. The

V. berus venoms and the effectiveness of two monovalent antivenoms in vivo in mice. The two antivenoms tested effectively counteract the effect of V. berus venom, but only partially neutralize the neurotoxicity of V. aspis , supporting the use of polyvalent antivenoms [ ]. Therefore, the use of polyvalent antivenoms against numerous species and subspecies of vipers could represent an interesting strategy for the more effective management of European snakes. Furthermore, small-molecule inhibitors that target the activity of the main toxic components of venoms can also be taken into account for the development of new broad-spectrum antivenoms [ ]. The antidote should ideally be administered via intravenous infusion; if this is not possible, it can be administered by slow intravenous push at a maximum rate of 2 mL/minute. The doses of antivenom in children and adults are the same, since the volume of venom injected does not depend on the size of the victim. However, the volume of saline in which the antivenom is diluted is generally lower in children to avoid fluid overload [ ]. An additional dose of antivenom can be administered if neurotoxicity or cardiocirculatory symptoms worsen or if bleeding persists 1–2 h following the initial dose [ ]. However, a recent systematic review of articles relating to antivenom in Europe showed that no randomized control trials comparing the effectiveness of antivenoms were carried out and clinical studies were mostly retrospective. Better and more systematic data, including randomized controlled trials comparing different antivenoms in Europe, are required to better assess the antivenoms’ effectiveness against different Vipera species [ ]. 6.4. Adverse Reactions to Antivenom Potential serious life-threatening reactions due to the use of foreign animal proteins derived from the immunized animal are the main issue with antidotes [ ]. Adverse reactions to antivenom can be classified into early and late reactions [ ]. Early reactions tend to be mild and include symptoms such as itching, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, headache or fever [ ]. However, in some cases, severe systemic anaphylaxis can occur, with bronchospasm, hypotension or angioedema [ ]. In one study, anaphylaxis occurred in 3.3% patients within 10–180 min after the administration of antivenom [ ]. These early reactions are likely caused by complement activation through immunoglobulin(Ig)-G aggregates present in equine serum [ ]. Modifying antivenoms through enzymatic digestion with papain or pepsin (which cleaves IgG) and the subsequent removal of the Fc region may reduce, but not completely eliminate, acute reactions [ ]. In cases of early reactions, subcutaneous adrenaline administration can be helpful. The incidence of early reactions varies, ranging from 2% to 50% of patients [ ]. Late reactions, similar to serum sickness, can occur 1–2 weeks after treatment. These are characterized by fever, itching, arthralgia, lymphadenopathy and albuminuria. They are caused by immune complexes and typically respond to treatment with corticosteroids and antihistamines [ ]. However, in literature, these reactions are mostly described after the administration of antivenom outside Europe. Data from a European systematic review showed that adverse reactions were reported in 37 of 2408 cases (1.5%), including 7 cases of anaphylaxis. Therefore, reported adverse reactions were rare, suggesting that modern intravenous antivenoms are of good quality [ ]. 6.5. Ancillary Therapy In addition to immunotherapy, ancillary measures and drugs may play a role in the management of viper bites. The involved skin area can be cleaned with hydrogen peroxide, potassium permanganate or plain water (viper venom is water-soluble) [ ]. Alcohol and other chemical substances should be avoided since toxic compounds can be generated [ ]. The use of tourniquets, cutting, sucking or scarifying the wound and the application of chemicals or electric shock are not recommended [ ]. It is essential to periodically evaluate vesicles and blisters, because they can hide underlying necrosis [ ]. Antibiotic usage is controversial and should be evaluated based on the patient’s medical history, physical examination and laboratory results [ ]. A swab of the affected area is recommended for diagnostic purposes [ ]. Corticosteroids should not be administered [ ] because they increase the risk of bacterial infections [ ]. Tetanus toxin and tetanus immunoglobulin should be administered to unvaccinated children. Ensuring adequate pain relief is crucial, even though some snake venoms cause little or no pain. In low- and middle-income countries, ketamine is commonly used for analgesia [ ], but paracetamol is preferable for analgesia in children [ ]. Nonsteroidal Anti-Inflammatory Drugs should be avoided due to their potential to increase bleeding risk [ ]. Despite the recommendations, a recent systematic review found that antibiotics (in 2009/3065 cases), steroids (in 1385/2480 cases) and antihistamines (in 913/1737 cases) were frequently administered. Notably, systemic steroids were frequently co-administered with antivenom. Many patients received fluids and analgesics, as well as heparin (139/1287 cases) and inotrope drugs (82/732 cases) [ ]. The use of anticoagulants in

little or no pain. In low- and middle-income countries, ketamine is commonly used for analgesia [ ], but paracetamol is preferable for analgesia in children [ ]. Nonsteroidal Anti-Inflammatory Drugs should be avoided due to their potential to increase bleeding risk [ ]. Despite the recommendations, a recent systematic review found that antibiotics (in 2009/3065 cases), steroids (in 1385/2480 cases) and antihistamines (in 913/1737 cases) were frequently administered. Notably, systemic steroids were frequently co-administered with antivenom. Many patients received fluids and analgesics, as well as heparin (139/1287 cases) and inotrope drugs (82/732 cases) [ ]. The use of anticoagulants in the treatment of viper bites remains controversial. Some studies suggest that low-molecular-weight heparin (LMWH) may increase the risk of hematoma and functional impairment, particularly when patients have received early envenomation treatment [ ]. A recent study by Boels et al. [ ] found that prophylactic administration of LMWH was significantly associated with longer hospital stays, exceeding 48 h. 7. Pediatric Viper-Bite Cases in Europe in Literature Most pediatric case series of snakebites have been conducted in India, Sri Lanka and other non-European countries, where this issue is more frequent. Snakes in Europe all belong to the genus true Vipera and lead to different clinical features compared to snakes such as pit vipers [ , ]. Information about snake envenomation in Europe is mainly derived from studies in adults. Recently, several case series and studies regarding European viper envenomation in children were reported in literature [ , , , , ]. These data helped in understanding the specific characteristics of snake venom envenomation in children in Europe and in developing specific tools, such as the pediatric grading severity score [ ]. Marano et al. [ ] retrospectively reviewed 24 cases of pediatric viper bites admitted to the Pediatric Emergency Department and the Pediatric Intensive Care Unit of the Bambino Gesù Children Hospital in Rome between 2000 and 2020. The median age of the patients was 4.2 years, with a male predominance (female-to-male ratio of 1:1.6), and most cases occurred in the late summer. All extremities were involved, with a slight predominance of the superior limbs (54.5%). The most frequent signs were pain, local edema and swelling, and no mortality was observed. Two patients presented neurological signs (ptosis and dysarthria or nystagmus). The authors also observed that a higher white blood cell count and an increase in the International Normalized Ratio, lactate dehydrogenase and C-reactive protein levels were associated with clinical severity. Antivenom administration was necessary in 12 cases, and 4 patients required a second dose; no significant side effects were reported, except in 1 case of serum sickness with a mild rash on both legs a week after the administration of the antivenom. Recently, the case of a 6-year-old Italian girl who experienced multiple viper bites in the lower limb and developed compartment syndrome was described. This case showed that a prompt assessment of the severity of viper envenomation and the administration of antivenom are essential in children [ ]. A French retrospective study, including 58 children (43 males) who arrived at the emergency department between 2001 and 2009 with a mean age of 8 years, documented that bites occurred mainly in the afternoon (62%) and mainly affected the lower limbs (77%). The degrees of envenomation were grades 0 and 1 in 83% of cases and grades 2 and 3 in 17% of cases [ ]. A potential association between initial hyperglycemia, being bitten on an upper extremity, being bitten during the afternoon and experiencing severe pain and the risk of progression to high-grade envenomation was found [ ] and confirmed in another retrospective study conducted between 2001 and 2014 with 83 children [ ]. Interestingly, a French electronic clinical tool (VipGrade ® ) useful to grade envenomations due to European Vipera and decide whether to use specific immunotherapy was created in 2022. However, a retrospective cohort of 116 children with Vipera envenomation showed a discordance of this tool with the initial grading assigned by clinicians on admission, notably in grade I, overgrading a substantial number of cases [ ]. A larger European pediatric cohort was investigated in a retrospective study of 160 children that experienced venomous snakebites in southern Croatia [ ]. The authors confirmed that most bites occurred from early May to late August and the greater involvement of upper limbs. Local complications were observed in 24% of children and included hemorrhagic blisters (20%) and compartment syndrome (7.5%). General complications were observed in 25% of patients and included cranial nerve paresis or paralysis (11.2%) and shock symptoms (7%). Only one child (0.6%) died because of snakebite directly on the neck. All patients received antivenom without an anaphylactic reaction. All patients also received tetanus prophylaxis, and almost all of them received antibiotics, corticosteroids and antihistamines [ ]. 8. Conclusions Being

Local complications were observed in 24% of children and included hemorrhagic blisters (20%) and compartment syndrome (7.5%). General complications were observed in 25% of patients and included cranial nerve paresis or paralysis (11.2%) and shock symptoms (7%). Only one child (0.6%) died because of snakebite directly on the neck. All patients received antivenom without an anaphylactic reaction. All patients also received tetanus prophylaxis, and almost all of them received antibiotics, corticosteroids and antihistamines [ ]. 8. Conclusions Being an uncommon event in Europe, viper envenomation can be misdiagnosed, and delayed recognition may delay appropriate management. Information about snake envenomation in Europe is mainly derived from studies in adults. A viper bite in children is rarely life-threatening, but it is particularly challenging due to the lower volume of distribution of venom in children compared to adults. Furthermore, symptoms could be heterogeneous and require close and careful monitoring for the onset of complications such as compartment syndrome. Although the venom of European vipers is considered mostly cytotoxic and hemotoxic, neurological symptoms are not so rare in children, especially affecting the cranial nerves. A protocol for the management of viper bites in Europe was proposed, but a tailored and standardized protocol for children is still needed. It is important that management in children differs from that in adults, given the greater dangerousness of snake venom, the different clinical characteristics and therapeutic management. Recently, efforts have been made to improve the pediatric approach to this issue. Several case reports in children were reported in literature, and a grading severity score for snakebitten children including the specific cutoff values of laboratory findings (e.g., white blood cells, neutrophil percentage) and specific management indications was created. Therefore, it is desirable that pediatricians use Audebert–Boels classification adapted to children by Marano et al. for the severity assessment and management of viper bites in children. Furthermore, larger studies are needed to validate the pediatric grading severity score and the VipGrade ® tool ( https://www.toxicologie-clinique.org/vipgrade-tool/ , accessed on 6 February 2025). Furthermore, the differences in venomous snake species and available resources (including antivenoms) in each country highlight the need for a national snakebite register and standardized protocols for each European country to optimize the management of snakebites in children in Europe.

chunks.content: INTRODUCTION Combat-related, polytraumatic wound infections are prevalent among combat casualties, and can complicate the recovery of wounded military personnel, contributing to overall morbidity and mortality. Trauma management for these patients becomes further complicated if multidrug-resistant bacteria are the primary cause of that infection. -- The ESKAPEE pathogens, including Enterococcus spp., Staphylococcus aureus, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Acinetobacter baumannii, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Escherichia coli , and Enterobacter spp., are a subset of opportunistic gram-positive and gram-negative bacteria, which are a common cause of wound infections and frequently found in both civilian and military hospitals. Multidrug-resistant gram-negative bacteria, such as E. coli, K. pneumoniae , and A. baumannii are also commonly seen in patients injured during combat operations and in complicated trauma management ; therefore, treatment of wounds with timely administration of antibiotics is key for reducing the risk of progression to sepsis or severe infections leading to amputation of extremities. In 2009, the Department of Defense and Veterans Affairs Trauma Infectious Disease Outcomes Study began enrolling patients to examine infectious disease outcomes in combat-injured U.S. Military personnel, with the goal of improving outcomes in military members with traumatic injuries. The study included patients with deployment-related injuries who had been admitted to two participating medical centers in the United States after medical evacuation from Iraq or Afghanistan via the Landstuhl Regional Medical Center in Germany. In an analysis of 2,699 deployment-related trauma patients, the overall infection rate in military personnel was 34% ( n = 913), where 543 patients had multidrug-resistant gram-negative infections ( E. coli , 48.3%; Acinetobacter spp., 38.6%; K. pneumoniae , 8.4%). Multidrug-resistant gram-negative infections occurred in a greater proportion of blast injuries (84.1% vs 62.5%), traumatic amputations (57.5% vs 16.3%), and higher injury severity (82.0% vs 33.7%) compared with non-multidrug-resistant gram-negative infections or no infection. The majority of patients received treatment with antibiotics from several common classes, including tetracyclines (78.4%), first-generation cephalosporins (73.5%), fluoroquinolones (46.5%), and vancomycin (42.4%). In contrast to the skin and soft-tissue infections seen in civilian clinical practice, there are a number of unique challenges to treating wound infections in a military context. First, infections following combat trauma differ clinically from those seen in general hospital admissions, as they are often associated with deep penetrating wounds and polytrauma including orthopedic trauma, extreme blood loss, burns, and/or head injuries. In addition, a key challenge faced within the military services is the continuum of care (Role I–V): combat medics generally administer emergency first aid in the field (Role I), and antibiotics are not often administered until patients have been evacuated to a battalion aid station (Role II) for stabilization and eventually transported to combat/regional hospitals for further medical care (Role III). -- In suitable patients, an orally administered antibiotic with broad spectrum activity is preferred for use in combat settings, where the facilities or the environment for intravenous administration may not be available. , Current treatment recommendations for combat-related injuries include the use of intravenous cefazolin for the majority of wounds, with intravenous levofloxacin or oral moxifloxacin) for penetrating eye injuries. Where casualties cannot be immediately transferred to hospital care, oral moxifloxacin can be administered for casualties without penetrating abdominal trauma, shock, or co-administration of other oral medications. With the growing problem of antibiotic resistance, and in particular beta-lactam and fluoroquinolone resistance, these recommendations come with a caveat of not being intended to treat nosocomial pathogens or multidrug-resistant pathogens. Ideally, the military needs a broad-spectrum antibiotic that can be used empirically and as early as possible in both combat and healthcare settings to prevent the primary infection, as well as potential nosocomial infections, and reduce the risk of developing sepsis. Treatment of infectious complications after combat trauma is specific to each patient, the site of infection, and the microorganism(s) involved. As with all wound infections, considerations for the optimal treatment include antimicrobial susceptibility profile against the suspected pathogen(s), the patient’s drug allergy/intolerance, drug distribution to the site of infection, monitoring requirements, dosing convenience or burden, potential drug–drug interactions, antimicrobial stewardship considerations, and cost of the drug. Current clinical practice guidelines (CPGs) recommend high-dose cefazolin with or without metronidazole as prophylaxis or ertapenem for most combat trauma, with oral moxifloxacin or intravenous/intramuscular/intraosseous ertapenem recommended at point of injury if there is an expected delay to surgical care. , CPGs are considered to be suitable recommendations for prophylactic treatment, as a review of outcomes showed that for every 10% increase in compliance, there was an associated 14% decrease in mortality risk, likely because of the better performance of cefazolin against gram-positive bacteria and bacteremia caused by those organisms. , However, beta-lactam-resistant, gram-negative pathogens can sometimes escape this regimen, leading to an increasing likelihood of infections with these organisms. , Given the limited spectrum of cefazolin, the significant increase in beta-lactam resistance, the potential for allergic reactions, and existing black box warnings for

an expected delay to surgical care. , CPGs are considered to be suitable recommendations for prophylactic treatment, as a review of outcomes showed that for every 10% increase in compliance, there was an associated 14% decrease in mortality risk, likely because of the better performance of cefazolin against gram-positive bacteria and bacteremia caused by those organisms. , However, beta-lactam-resistant, gram-negative pathogens can sometimes escape this regimen, leading to an increasing likelihood of infections with these organisms. , Given the limited spectrum of cefazolin, the significant increase in beta-lactam resistance, the potential for allergic reactions, and existing black box warnings for metronidazole and the fluoroquinolones, , there remains an unmet need for alternative treatment options. Omadacycline is an aminomethylcycline antibiotic that may have the potential to address some of the unmet needs in treating wound and skin infections within the military. It was FDA-approved in 2018 for treatment of adults with acute bacterial skin and skin structure infections (ABSSSI), as well as community-acquired bacterial pneumonia (CABP), and is available as a once-daily intravenous or oral formulation. Omadacycline has a broad spectrum of activity against aerobic and anaerobic gram-positive, gram-negative, and atypical bacteria. , As with other third-generation tetracyclines, omadacycline is not affected by the most common tetracycline-class resistance mechanisms, tet efflux pumps and ribosomal protection proteins. This review will discuss the potential role of omadacycline, which is included in the Department of Defense Formulary, in the context of combat wound infections. METHODS PubMed was searched with the following search string “omadacycline AND (acute bacterial skin and skin structure infections OR skin infection OR community acquired bacterial pneumonia OR pneumonia OR in vitro activity OR in vivo OR biothreat OR sexually transmitted pathogens OR rickettsia) AND (Enterococcus faecium OR Staphylococcus aureus OR Klebsiella pneumoniae, OR Acinetobacter baumannii OR Pseudomonas aeruginosa OR Enterobacter spp. OR Escherichia coli OR C. difficile)” for any studies published before July 21, 2023. In addition to this, the bibliography publicly available on the Paratek Pharmaceuticals, Inc. website was reviewed. A limited number of studies focused on the military; consequently, the search was expanded to include the civilian population. Publications presenting primary data published in English on omadacycline in relation to ESKAPEE pathogens and C. difficile, including in vitro, in vivo , and clinical data were included in the evidence review. RESULTS shows the outcome of the literature search. Of 260 identified records, 66 studies describing in vitro, in vivo, and clinical studies were eligible for inclusion in the evidence review. In Vitro <italic toggle="yes">and</italic> In Vivo Activity Omadacycline has in vitro activity against almost all the ESKAPEE pathogens, except for P. aeruginosa . Importantly, it has activity against the four most prevalent bacterial pathogens that have caused wound infections in military healthcare system (MHS) patients in the most recent conflicts: S. aureus , including methicillin-resistant S. aureus (MRSA), -- A. baumannii , , , K. pneumoniae , , , and E. coli , , ( ). Minimum inhibitory concentrations inhibiting 50% (MIC 50 ) and 90% (MIC 90 ) of isolates tested have been observed previously at 0.12 and 0.25 mg/L, respectively, against S. aureus (including MRSA). Recently, our team analyzed the in vitro activity of omadacycline against panels of 100 bacterial strains each of genetically and geographically diverse A. baumannii and K. pneumoniae derived from clinical isolates collected worldwide. Clinical isolates were provided from beneficiaries and other individuals by the Walter Reed Army Institute of Research’s Multidrug-Resistant Organism Repository and Surveillance Network (MRSN). Omadacycline demonstrated an MIC 50 and MIC 90 value of 0.5 and 2.0 mg/L, respectively, against A. baumannii , and an MIC 50 and MIC 90 value of 2.0 and 8.0 mg/L, respectively, against K. pneumoniae , and with potency superior to the MIC 90 obtained for doxycycline as the tested comparator tetracycline drug. , In vivo estimates of tissue exposure in patients with wound infections (diabetic foot infection) and healthy volunteers have demonstrated mean area under the curve tissue values of 0.82 and 1.37 mg*h/L, respectively, supporting data from other pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic analyses of omadacycline. Clinical Efficacy The clinical efficacy of omadacycline has been assessed in three Phase 3 studies in patients with ABSSSI (OASIS-1 and OASIS-2) and with CABP (OPTIC). -- In both OASIS-1 and OPTIC, patients were started on intravenous omadacycline, with the option to switch to an oral formulation after 3 days of treatment. , OASIS-2 evaluated an oral-only formulation of omadacycline, with once-daily administration of 300 mg omadacycline following two initial 450 mg oral loading doses. In all three studies, omadacycline was found to be non-inferior to the comparator drug for early clinical response , for the skin infection studies, this was defined as survival with at least a 20% reduction in lesion size 48 to 72 h after the first dose without the need for rescue therapy. , Post-hoc

OASIS-1 and OPTIC, patients were started on intravenous omadacycline, with the option to switch to an oral formulation after 3 days of treatment. , OASIS-2 evaluated an oral-only formulation of omadacycline, with once-daily administration of 300 mg omadacycline following two initial 450 mg oral loading doses. In all three studies, omadacycline was found to be non-inferior to the comparator drug for early clinical response , for the skin infection studies, this was defined as survival with at least a 20% reduction in lesion size 48 to 72 h after the first dose without the need for rescue therapy. , Post-hoc analysis of pooled data from the two skin infection studies assessed the efficacy of omadacycline vs linezolid specifically in patients with wound infections who did not inject drugs. -- Overall, 66% to 78% of patients across the treatment groups had wounds from recent trauma. Comparable clinical success was observed between the two treatments and to the overall study population in both early clinical response and post-treatment evaluation against wound infections positive for monomicrobial gram-positive, polymicrobial gram-positive, and polymicrobial mixed (gram-positive and gram-negative) pathogens ( ). -- SAFETY AND TOLERABILITY Adverse Events Overall, omadacycline has an established safety profile in the treatment of both ABSSSI and CABP. In patients with skin infections, the most commonly occurring adverse events (AEs) were nausea and vomiting ( ). , In the two Phase 3 omadacycline studies in which patients were started on intravenous therapy, the rates of nausea and vomiting observed with omadacycline were similar to the comparators linezolid and moxifloxacin. A higher rate of nausea and vomiting was observed with omadacycline in the oral-only OASIS-2 study, which was predominantly associated with the 450 mg loading dose used in the first 2 days of the study. In OASIS-2, of the patients reporting nausea and vomiting, 50% of patients receiving omadacycline (60/120) and 40% of those receiving linezolid (12/30) used concomitant antiemetics. , Despite the higher rates of nausea and vomiting observed in OASIS-2, gastrointestinal AEs were mostly transient, mild-to-moderate in severity, and were not treatment limiting. Importantly, across the three phase 3 trials only four patients (0.4%) discontinued omadacycline treatment because of gastrointestinal AEs. -- Drug–drug Interactions Both in vitro and in vivo data suggest omadacycline has a low potential for drug–drug interactions. As tetracyclines have been noted to depress plasma prothrombin activity, the potential exists for drug–drug interactions with anticoagulant therapy, which may require downward dose adjustments if taken in combination with omadacycline. In addition, absorption of oral tetracyclines, including omadacycline, is impaired by antacids containing aluminum, calcium, or magnesium, bismuth subsalicylate, and iron-containing preparations. DISCUSSION The etiology of skin and soft-tissue infections seen in combat settings differs from that of the civilian population, particularly regarding the prevalence of gram-negative pathogens. This review focused on omadacycline, but other antibiotics which have been approved or in are development for ABSSSI may also have unique properties and attributes of benefit to the military. Some of these have also been evaluated in DoD-funded research laboratories. Since 2010, six drugs have been approved for ABSSSI (dalbavancin, oritavancin, tedizolid, ceftaroline, delafloxacin, and omadacycline), although only the latter three have any gram-negative activity. Further to this, only 11 of 43 pipeline antibiotics in clinical development are projected to be candidates for an ABSSSI indication. Thus, more action is needed given the increases in antibiotic resistance, the lack of gram-negative activity in the pipeline agents, and the lack of a relevant clinical indication. In addition to the consideration of newly FDA-approved antibiotics, military-funded laboratories are also exploring what are considered non-traditional antibacterial approaches, such as monoclonal antibodies, bacteriophage, antimicrobial peptides, antibiotic adjuvants, and predatory bacteria. Tetracycline-class Drugs Although tetracyclines share many characteristics, such as a broad spectrum of activity, there are certain characteristics that differ among the individual agents, including those related to treatment and dosing ( ). Newer tetracycline-class drugs, including omadacycline, overcome the most common tetracycline resistance mechanisms, resulting in higher rates of organism susceptibility compared with older agents ( ). In general, the newer tetracyclines have prolonged half-lives compared with the older drugs, allowing once- or twice-daily administration. Concentration-dependent gastrointestinal AEs associated with eravacycline and tigecycline support administration twice daily. , Omadacycline exhibits higher and more sustained concentrations in plasma, epithelial lining fluid, and alveolar cells compared with tigecycline, such that the systemic exposure of omadacycline is approximately threefold higher than that of tigecycline. A number of AEs have been reported for other tetracycline-class drugs, such as photosensitivity, pseudotumor cerebri, and anti-anabolic action, although these reactions vary across individual agents. Because omadacycline is structurally similar to other tetracycline-class drugs, the potential risk of phototoxicity was evaluated in in vitro assays in mammalian cells. In these assays, omadacycline did not fulfill the criteria for a clear phototoxic response, demonstrating an in vitro phototoxicity profile similar to that of

concentrations in plasma, epithelial lining fluid, and alveolar cells compared with tigecycline, such that the systemic exposure of omadacycline is approximately threefold higher than that of tigecycline. A number of AEs have been reported for other tetracycline-class drugs, such as photosensitivity, pseudotumor cerebri, and anti-anabolic action, although these reactions vary across individual agents. Because omadacycline is structurally similar to other tetracycline-class drugs, the potential risk of phototoxicity was evaluated in in vitro assays in mammalian cells. In these assays, omadacycline did not fulfill the criteria for a clear phototoxic response, demonstrating an in vitro phototoxicity profile similar to that of the non-phototoxic tetracycline minocycline (data on file, Paratek Pharmaceuticals, Inc.). In addition, in Phase 3 clinical trials, no patient receiving omadacycline had an AE of photosensitivity. -- Omadacycline has been studied in a limited number of clinical trials and it is possible rare AEs have not been identified. Therefore, the ongoing pharmacovigilance program is critical. Although tigecycline carries a black box warning for all-cause mortality, there was no increase in mortality observed for omadacycline vs linezolid in skin infection studies (0.1% vs 0.4%). In the phase 3 CABP study, there was an imbalance in mortality between omadacycline and the comparator moxifloxacin groups (8 patients [2%] vs 4 patients [1%]). The cause of this imbalance is unknown, but mortality rates in both groups were consistent with the expected range (1%–3%) based on other recently conducted CABP registration trials. , Tetracycline-class drugs are associated with lower rates of C. difficile infection compared with other classes of antibiotics, such as fluoroquinolones and third-generation cephalosporins. Similar to other tetracyclines, omadacycline has potent in vitro activity against C. difficile . The potential mechanisms by which tetracyclines confer a lower risk of C. difficile infection may include high drug concentrations in the bowel or reduced disruption to gut microbiota compared with other antibiotics. POTENTIAL ROLE OF OMADACYCLINE IN THE MILITARY Potential Benefits Currently, moxifloxacin is often carried and used by combat medics in the Combat Wound Medication Packet (CWMP), and it can be added to the military Individual First Aid Kit (IFAK). -- Omadacycline could be an attractive replacement for moxifloxacin or an addition to both the CWMP and IFAK, specifically because of its oral formulation and broad spectrum of activity, given increasing resistance observed to fluoroquinolones and carbapenems. The storage conditions of medication in the CWMP and IFAK must also be considered. Omadacycline is packaged in aluminum foil blister packs containing desiccant that provides an impermeable moisture barrier via cross-diffusion through the blister edges and can be stored at room temperature (20–25 °C [68–77°F]). Stability of both tablets and IV vials without any signs of degradation has been demonstrated when stored at 50 °C for up to 72 h, making it suitable for many different environments encountered by soldiers. In long-term analysis, the stability of omadacycline tablets has been confirmed for 36 months at 25 °C and 60% relative humidity, and 6 months in more extreme conditions (40 °C/75% relative humidity). Omadacycline’s once-daily administration and broad spectrum of activity across multiple pathogens allows a combat medic to potentially carry fewer drugs to treat a bacterial infection, leaving room for other important supplies. In addition, renal clearance of tetracycline-class drugs is lower than that seen for standard-of-care cefazolin (60–80%). Because augmented renal clearance by glomerular hyperfiltration is known to occur in young, male, otherwise healthy patients with significant trauma injuries, drugs with lower renal clearance are preferred as they would not require dose alterations. This could provide a substantial benefit of omadacycline over current standard-of-care drugs. Potential for Additional Uses in the Military Outside of Wound Infections In addition to its potential for wound infections, omadacycline has other attributes that are relevant to the military. Omadacycline has demonstrated in vitro activity against bioterrorism pathogens, including Bacillus anthracis, Burkholderia mallei, Francisella tularensis , and Yersinia pestis ; and in murine models, omadacycline demonstrated significantly greater efficacy vs vehicle controls in treatment of aerosolized B. anthracis and as post-exposure prophylaxis for Y. pestis . , Omadacycline has also demonstrated in vitro activity against bacterial pathogens that cause sexually transmitted infections (STI), including Neisseria gonorrhoeae, Chlamydia trachomatis , and Mycoplasma genitalium ; and although further research is needed, these data suggest that omadacycline could provide an alternative oral treatment option for STI, including in patients with multiple infections. , In addition, in vitro activity of omadacycline has also been demonstrated against multiple Rickettsia species, and presents a potentially attractive treatment option as an oral agent, particularly in Rocky Mountain spotted fever-endemic regions where intravenous doxycycline, the current standard of care, is not available. Finally, tetracycline-class drugs are also frequently used by the military as prophylaxis against malaria, and further study on the potential activity of omadacycline against Plasmodium falciparum is warranted. Remaining Challenges As omadacycline clinical efficacy in the

data suggest that omadacycline could provide an alternative oral treatment option for STI, including in patients with multiple infections. , In addition, in vitro activity of omadacycline has also been demonstrated against multiple Rickettsia species, and presents a potentially attractive treatment option as an oral agent, particularly in Rocky Mountain spotted fever-endemic regions where intravenous doxycycline, the current standard of care, is not available. Finally, tetracycline-class drugs are also frequently used by the military as prophylaxis against malaria, and further study on the potential activity of omadacycline against Plasmodium falciparum is warranted. Remaining Challenges As omadacycline clinical efficacy in the combat setting and in prolonged care situations has not been established challenges remain, particularly for pathogens, such as Acinetobacter spp. In addition, omadacycline lacks activity against P. aeruginosa. Moreover, branded drugs are typically priced higher than generic drugs, and so the higher cost of omadacycline compared with current standard of care, moxifloxacin, may be a barrier to its implementation in the military setting without additional justification for use. In addition, as with all antibiotics, the potential for the development of resistance in normal flora and indicated or opportunistic pathogens should be considered. Although the most common tetracycline resistance is overcome by new tetracyclines, such as omadacycline, the most concerning mechanism is a flavin-dependent monooxygenase encoded by the tet (X) gene that has been identified on mobile elements. Tet (X) confers resistance to all tetracycline-class drugs, including tigecycline, eravacycline, and omadacycline. Resistance to omadacycline has not been reported in the United States via this mechanism, but tet (X) gene variants conveying high-level resistance to tigecycline have been detected in China. To the best of our knowledge, the prevalence of tet (X) currently appears low. CONCLUSIONS Omadacycline offers the potential for broad-spectrum activity against multiple wound-associated pathogens including S. aureus, S. pneumoniae, E. coli, A. baumannii , and K. pneumoniae and is not affected by the most common tetracycline resistance mechanisms associated with resistance to earlier tetracycline-class drugs. In addition, omadacycline’s activity against known bioterrorism pathogens, bacteria that cause STI, and Rickettsia , as well as its potential activity against malaria, there is potential clinical utility in the MHS because of the ability to combat multiple threats simultaneously. Clinical data from thousands of civilian patients suggest an established safety profile, with potential benefits over the currently recommended antibiotics, such as clindamycin, metronidazole, and the fluoroquinolones, which all have black box warnings. The oral formulation of omadacycline, together with its high stability, makes the drug a potential addition or replacement antibiotic in the current soldier IFAK. Omadacycline could then play an important role in the treatment of cases that may require prolonged care, i.e., those patients facing delayed surgical care, and ultimately reduce the risk of sepsis through prevention or progression of wound infection. Although adherence to antimicrobial treatments is estimated at 50–60% in the military with combat-related injuries, far higher than in civilian settings, the once-daily oral formulation would also aid in regimen adherence. Although there remain several questions about the use of omadacycline in the military setting, including current clinical indications, lack of activity against P. aeruginosa , and the potential for the development of resistance, omadacycline offers several potential benefits for the treatment of resistant wound-associated pathogens and could be a useful solution until other, new antibiotics are developed and FDA-approved. Further testing and evaluation and clinical evidence is warranted to support broader use of omadacycline to treat combat wound infections in the field and hospital settings for potential inclusion in the U.S. Military CPGs. chunks.content: Introduction At high altitudes, which typically exceed 2500 m, approximately 80 million people reside permanently, with over one million visitors annually for tourism, sports, religion or work. The largest populations of permanent residents at high altitudes are found in the Andes of South America, the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau, the Caucasus of Eastern Europe, Ethiopia, and the Himalayas. In recent years, an increasing number of people, especially the older population, have been drawn to such areas, including trekkers, climbers, miners, military personnel, astronomers, and athletes undergoing sports training. Both native highlanders and newcomers are at risk of high-altitude disease. The incidence and severity of high-altitude disease are determined by the attained altitude, ascent variables (including environmental and behavioral factors), and individual susceptibility. Owing to these factors, as well as diverse study designs and biases, the exact prevalence of altitude sickness among unacclimatized lowlanders and highlanders remains uncertain. The major effect of high altitude on human physiology is a decrease in partial oxygen pressure and content in the circulating blood, which is directly associated with the reduction in barometric pressure that occurs with ascent. Hypoxia, i.e., diminished oxygen availability, is defined as a decrease in the partial pressure of oxygen compared with normal status in the blood, organs, tissue, or cells. Hypoxic stress at high altitude can trigger a series of physiological responses across multiple organ systems, especially the brain (increased cerebral blood flow), pulmonary system (increased ventilation and pulmonary vascular remodeling), cardiovascular system (increased heart rate, cardiac output, and systemic blood pressure), renal system (increased bicarbonate excretion and erythropoietin (EPO) secretion), and hematologic system (increased red cell mass, hemoglobin (Hb) concentration, and hematocrit (Hct)), thereby increasing oxygen content and delivery in the body. , These compensatory adaptive changes are collectively referred to as acclimatization, which enables individuals to work and live at high altitude without any discomfort. An inadequate or excessive compensatory adaptive response, termed malacclimatization, can impair oxygen delivery, leading to hypoxemia, which is defined as a decrease in the arterial partial pressure of oxygen (PaO₂). Hypoxemia is a well-known primary cause of high-altitude illness among many visitors, sojourners, and natives. , High-altitude hypoxia-related diseases include acute mountain sickness (AMS, also known asacute mild altitude disease (AMAD)), high-altitude cerebral edema (HACE), high-altitude pulmonary edema (HAPE), chronic mountain sickness (CMS), high-altitude pulmonary hypertension (HAPH; also known as high-altitude heart disease, HAHD), high-altitude deterioration (HAD), etc. , Acute altitude illnesses (e.g., AMS, HACE, and HAPE) result from inadequate physiological adaptation to hypobaric hypoxia, whereas chronic conditions such as HAPH and CMS reflect the pathological consequences of prolonged or excessive adaptive responses. Within h to 5 days of exposure to hypobaric hypoxia, some individuals are susceptible to acute altitude illness, including mild (AMS) and severe (HAPE and HACE) forms (Fig. ). The symptoms of AMS, a self-limiting and nonfatal disease, are usually nonspecific and include headache with any of the following: poor appetite or nausea/vomiting, fatigue or lassitude, and dizziness/light-headedness. AMS can progress to a potentially lethal illness, HACE, associated with neurological signs, such as truncal ataxia, altered mental status, depressed consciousness, and encephalopathy. HAPE, a noncardiogenic pulmonary edema and the most fatal form of acute altitude illness, is characterized by dyspnea, loss of stamina, and dry cough, followed by dyspnea at rest, cyanosis, gurgling in the chest and pink frothy sputum. Natives or long-term high-altitude sojourners, who are chronically exposed to altitude hypoxia, may develop several altitude-related illnesses, including polycythemia, systemic hypertension, pulmonary hypertension, congenital heart disease, thromboembolic disease, lung disease, mental deterioration, as well as pregnancy and neonatal problems. There is a consensus that CMS (or Monge’s disease) and HAPH are the most common forms of chronic altitude illness (Fig. ). CMS, which is more prevalent among Andeans than Tibetans, is characterized by excessive erythrocytosis (females Hb ≥19 g/dL, males Hb ≥21 g/dL) and severe hypoxemia, and is frequently associated with neurological symptoms, pulmonary hypertension, and impaired pulmonary ventilation/perfusion. , HAPH, which occurs in high-altitude adults, is defined by a mean pulmonary artery pressure (mPAP) > 30 mmHg or a systolic pulmonary artery pressure (sPAP) > 50 mmHg, and is generally associated with right ventricular hypertrophy, heart failure, moderate hypoxemia, and the absence of excessive erythrocytosis. HAD symptoms broadly include weight loss, poor appetite, slow recovery from fatigue, lethargy, irritability, lack of willpower to start new tasks, slowed mental processes, dull affect, and impaired cognitive function. Currently, there is still a lack of consensus regarding the diagnosis or management of HAD, making it challenging to accurately delineate its prevalence and pathogenic mechanisms. John B West has skilfully documented the history of high altitude medicine and physiology, highlighting key observations, experiments, and challenges. Although AMS has been known for more than a century, its diagnostic standard was only established at the 1991 International Hypoxia Symposium in Banff, Canada. Recent studies have revealed that “difficulty sleeping”, one of the five symptoms scored for AMS, is more of an effect of hypoxia than closely related to other AMS symptoms, thereby removing the sleep component from the Lake Louise AMS score in 2018. HACE was originally described by Ravenhill et al. and officially named by Fitch. The 2024 Wilderness Medical Society (WMS) Practice Guidelines updated the definition of HACE as severe AMS with neurological signs. HAPE, often misdiagnosed as acute pneumonia before 1960, was first reported by Dr Charles Houston and later identified as noncardiogenic pulmonary edema by Hultgren et al. At the 1998 meeting of the International Society of Mountain Medicine (ISMM) in Matsumoto, Japan, an international consensus statement on CMS was developed. CMS was first described by Carlos Monge in 1928. A more recent consensus statement was developed at the 2004 ISMM meeting in Xining, China, in which the Qinghai CMS score enables quantitative assessment of CMS severity and comparison of CMS cases within or among different countries. HAPH was first documented by Wu and Liu in 1955, and since then, Chinese investigators have extensively used this term. It is necessary to differentiate HAPH from subacute mountain sickness (SAMS), which is rarely seen in adults but mainly occurs in infants. With an increasing global demand for recreation and habitation at high altitudes, people, especially travelers, altitude residents, physicians, or paramedical personnel, need to be familiar with symptom recognition and the pathogenic mechanisms of high altitude-related sickness, so that appropriate and novel prevention and treatment methods can be adopted to reduce the severity or morbidity. In this narrative review, we briefly summarize the clinical characteristics, major events, and epidemiology of high-altitude disease; focus on the pathophysiological changes, genetic susceptibility and potential mechanisms involved in altitude hypoxia-related sickness; and detail the preventive and therapeutic advances in animal experiments, clinical trials, and clinical experience. Epidemiology and risk factors for altitude illness Acute altitude illness The primary determinant of high-altitude hypoxia-related sickness is the altitude reached. Since HACE is rarely reported, systematic analysis of its risk factors is still lacking. HACE often begins as a severe form of AMS, suggesting that the determinants of HACE may be similar to those of AMS. , The major risk factors for AMS, HACE, and HAPE include altitude attained (especially the sleeping altitude), ascent rate, individual susceptibility, and degree of preacclimatisation. , Other risk factors for high-altitude illness include preexisting diseases, cold weather, fatigue, exercise, obesity, sex, and age. Several preexisting diseases, particularly cardiopulmonary diseases (such as pulmonary hypertension and bleeding disorders), may increase susceptibility to high-altitude disease. Globally, the reported prevalence of AMS, HACE, and HAPE varies significantly due to differences in these confounding variables, as well as study designs and biases. The prevalence of AMS generally depends on the altitude attained and speed of ascent. The incidence of AMS increases significantly with elevation. At 2000 m, only 12% of the subjects exhibited symptoms ; at 3050 and 3506 m, 75–79% of the unacclimatized persons experienced symptoms ; and at 3800 and 4310 m, nearly all the individuals experienced some symptoms. In the Western Alps, the AMS incidence was 9%, 13%, 34%, and 53% at altitudes of 2850, 3050, 3650, and 4559 m, respectively, whereas in the Eastern Alps, it was 6.9%, 9.1%, 17.4%, and 38.0% at 2200, 2500, 2800, and 3500 m, respectively. , In addition, the AMS prevalence is positively correlated with the rate of ascent. When individuals ascended to similar altitudes, gradual climbing allowed for partial acclimatization, resulting in a lower incidence (50% versus 84%) and less severity. The differences in susceptibility to AMS between males and females remain unclear, with conflicting reports. Hou et al. revealed that females tend to develop AMS, whereas others reported that men were slightly more affected by AMS than women. AMS is more common in children and younger individuals than older people aged >40–60 years, , although a recent meta-analysis revealed no association between age and AMS risk.
